author: Vikram Pandey
text:
Token Economics of #Resume Parsing: A Satire
रेज़्यूमे तो AI ने लिखा, पर इंटरव्यू में टोकन ख़त्म हो गए। 😆 

Had seen your Job Description… My AI engine ensured every keyword was patched in correctly -“Agile,” “Blockchain,” “Leadership,” “Agentic,” “Builder” sprinkled like masala on a street‑side chaat.
Then you receive the resume. You “spend tokens” to parse it… only to discover the exact same keywords, deliberately fed in for you to see.
Simple Use Case of Token Misutilisation 😉
The Comedy of Resume Parsing
Recruiter:  “Wow, this candidate knows Agile, Scrum, Kanban, DevOps, Cloud, AI, ML, NLP, IoT, AR/VR, and maybe even UFO engineering.” Reality: Candidate just ran a keyword patch script. AI Parser: “Thank you for your 1,500 tokens. Here’s a JSON file confirming the candidate knows… Agile, Scrum, Kanban…” Outcome: Zero new insight. Maximum token burn.
Classic Misuses – Don’t Tell Me You Realised It Now.

Buzzword Bingo: Resume reads like a startup pitch deck — “Disruption, Innovation, Unicorn, Synergy.”
Copy‑Paste Certifications: Same AWS certificate pasted thrice in different fonts.
Job Title Inflation: “Global Technology Evangelist” = Intern who once reset a router.
Skill Overload: Candidate lists 47 programming languages but can’t debug a print statement.
#Leadership/#Management
If your hiring funnel is just keyword‑matching, you’re not building teams you’re building token sinks.
 Winning organisations aren’t those that parse resumes faster; they’re those that filter noise smarter.
The real differentiator is not how many resumes you parse, but how many leaders you groom.

Closing Thought
We built AI to parse resumes. Candidates built AI to stuff resumes. Recruiters now spend tokens to confirm what they already suspected: the resume was engineered for the parser, not for the job.
💡 For CHROs and CXOs: The organisations that win are not those that “burn tokens” on parsing, but those that re‑engineer hiring to spot substance over syntax. Because fixing the hiring process is the first step to fixing the leadership pipeline , and that’s how winning teams are built.

author: Jacek Lonc
text:
Most AI projects don’t fail because the technology is broken – they fail because the team structure is. 

Building a high-impact AI team requires more than just hiring a "data scientist" and hoping for the best. AI delivery isn't a solo sport – it’s a cross-functional relay between data engineers, ML specialists and product managers. 

In the current market, the math is getting difficult. High-level AI talent in the US is not only expensive but has a notoriously long hiring cycle. Trying to build this entire ecosystem in-house from day one makes for a fertile ground for a bottleneck. 

This is why the hybrid model is becoming the default for fast-moving companies.  

It really comes down to agility. This means being flexible enough to plug in the expertise needed to turn AI into a measurable business outcome. Filling critical skill gaps on demand allows you to move from a "what if" prototype to a "live" system months ahead of your competitors.

AWS vs Azure vs GCP: Which Cloud Is Right for You?

“Just go with AWS. Everyone uses AWS.” The CTO closed the laptop. The evaluation was over before it started.

I see this in boardrooms across Pakistan, the UAE, and the US: the cloud platform decision made on reflex, vendor preference, or whoever shouted loudest in the architecture meeting. And it costs real money because the platform shapes architecture, hiring, and infrastructure spend for the next five to seven years.

💸Here’s the number that surprises most engineering leaders: for equivalent workloads, the cost difference between AWS, Azure, and GCP is typically only 5–15%. The decision rarely turns on raw price. It turns on what you’re actually building, who you’re hiring, and what you already run.

📋Five factors decide which platform fits your business, in this order:

⚙️Existing technology investments: Microsoft 365 / Windows / .NET → Azure cuts integration costs. Google Workspace + containers → GCP. No allegiance → AWS gives the broadest selection.

🧠Primary workload type: data analytics & ML favor GCP. Enterprise apps with Microsoft dependencies favor Azure. Broadest service catalog → AWS.

👥Team expertise: the platform your team already knows ships months earlier. Retraining is a real line item in TCO.

🌍Geographic requirements: map customer locations, data residency, and latency against each provider’s regional footprint (and consider Alibaba Cloud for APAC/MENA).

♟️Long-term vendor strategy: for most organizations, a single cloud with a documented exit plan beats multi-cloud price shopping.

🛍️Real engagement, UAE e-commerce client (~60 engineers, ~$30M revenue): leadership had pre-committed to AWS. Our structured evaluation surfaced a 22% TCO advantage for analytics on GCP BigQuery while the commerce stack stayed on AWS, where the team’s expertise lived. Hybrid AWS + GCP architecture, daily incremental sync.

📈Year-one outcomes: –18% net infrastructure cost, with +6% engineering operational overhead, a trade-off leadership consciously accepted because the math made sense for that workload. A vendor-aligned consultancy would never have surfaced the GCP finding.

🧩AWS leads in service breadth. Azure on enterprise integration. GCP on data and ML. There’s no universally “best” cloud, only the one that fits your workloads, your team, and your geography. 

We published a vendor-neutral comparison on Medium with the five-factor framework and the full case study. Link in the first comment 👇.

LinkedIn's 2026 data just confirmed something I've been feeling all year: AI Engineer is now the #1 fastest-growing job title in the US, with AI/ML postings up 74% year-over-year. But here's what nobody's mentioning — backend and infrastructure engineers are still the largest hiring category by raw volume.

Translation: the market isn't replacing generalist engineers with AI specialists. It's rewarding people who can do both.

Four things I've noticed job-hunting and building across Flutter, Node.js, and Supabase this year:

1. "AI experience" increasingly just means shipping n8n/LLM automations that save real hours — I built multilingual (Arabic/English/Turkish) chatbot workflows for an agency, and it opened more doors than any certificate did.

2. Security engineering listings are up 124% year-over-year. Auth and data handling aren't afterthoughts anymore — they're interview questions.

3. Solo-shipped projects still beat portfolio pieces. A live App Store submission with real users and reviews (SOUQAK, 5.0 rating) gets more traction in conversations than any resume line.

4. Full-stack plus automation is becoming the actual "AI skill" companies want, not prompt engineering alone.

The market seems to reward breadth with one deep specialty, not the other way around.
